nameStory: Wild bergamot gets its name from its wonderfully aromatic leaves that smell similar to the bergamot citrus used to flavor Earl Grey tea. However, this minty wildflower is completely unrelated to true bergamot - it just happens to share that distinctive, citrusy-herbal fragrance that made early settlers think of the precious imported spice.
description: Wild bergamot is a native wildflower that stands 2-4 feet tall with distinctive crowns of pink to lavender tubular flowers that bloom in summer. Like other members of the mint family, it has square stems and opposite leaves that release a delightful citrusy-mint fragrance when crushed. This hardy perennial spreads by underground runners and often forms patches in sunny, open areas throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, rounded clusters of pink to lavender tubular flowers crown each stem, looking like a spiky pincushion. Each individual flower is about an inch long with a distinctive two-lipped opening that bees love to crawl into.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves grow in opposite pairs up the stem and release a strong, pleasant citrus-mint aroma when rubbed between your fingers. The leaves have slightly toothed edges and a somewhat rough texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square stems that feel distinctly four-sided when rolled between your fingers - a telltale sign of the mint family. Plants typically reach 2-4 feet tall and often grow in loose colonies.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry nutlets develop after flowering, tucked within the persistent flower bracts that turn brown and papery by late summer.

habitat: Wild bergamot thrives in sunny, well-drained soils including prairies, old fields, roadsides, and woodland edges throughout New England. It's particularly common in disturbed areas and can tolerate poor, rocky soils where many other wildflowers struggle. You'll often find it growing alongside goldenrod, asters, and other native prairie plants.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as square-stemmed shoots with aromatic leaves. Young plants are already quite fragrant when leaves are crushed.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, when the distinctive pink-lavender flower heads are most prominent and buzzing with bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads that persist into autumn. Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back, but the square stems remain visible.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to the ground, leaving only dried stems and seed heads. Underground runners survive to produce new shoots in spring.

funFact: Native Americans called this plant 'Oswego tea' and used it as a caffeine-free tea substitute during the Boston Tea Party boycotts - it was literally the patriotic drink of choice during the American Revolution!
confusionNotes: Wild bergamot can be confused with other summer wildflowers, but the combination of square stems, opposite aromatic leaves, and distinctive spiky flower clusters makes it unmistakable. Remember: if it doesn't smell minty-citrusy when you crush a leaf, it's not wild bergamot.
contextualKnowledge: Despite sharing the name 'bergamot' with the citrus fruit that flavors Earl Grey tea, wild bergamot is completely unrelated to that Mediterranean citrus tree. The name confusion arose because both plants share similar aromatic compounds that produce that distinctive citrusy-herbal scent.
compareHints: Wild bergamot differs from its flashier cousin scarlet beebalm by its pink-lavender flowers (versus bright red) and its preference for drier soils. Unlike spotted horsemint, wild bergamot lacks the distinctive spotted bracts below its flowers and has a much more pleasant, citrusy fragrance rather than a harsh, medicinal smell.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While wild bergamot and scarlet beebalm flaunt bright purple and red flowers respectively, spotted horsemint keeps a lower profile with cream-colored blooms.
Scarlet beebalm is easily distinguished from its cousin wild bergamot by its brilliant red flowers (wild bergamot has pale pink or lavender blooms) and preference for moister soils.
Unlike scarlet beebalm's bright red flowers or wild bergamot's pale pink-purple blooms, lemon beebalm has distinctly tiered purple flower clusters.
Among New England's bergamots, purple bergamot is unique for its wetland habitat and reddish-purple flowers.
